newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: World Bank aids Sri Lanka private infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: World Bank aids Sri Lanka private infrastructure.

text.p: The World Bank is helping Sri Lanka's private sector develop the country's creaking infrastructure and attract the foreign investment needed to tackle unemployment, a senior official said on Monday.

The bank would help fund the Public Sector Infrastructure Development Co Ltd (PSID), a state-owned company set up to provide long-term subordinated debt to private sector projects, said Rohini Nanayakkara, general manager and chief executive officer of PSID.
"There is an urgent need to improve power, highways, ports, telecommunications, transport, solid waste management and water supply and drainage, as national priorities," she said.

"Improving infrastructure is the only way in which we can get the big foreign investment which is needed to relieve unemployment," said Nanayakkara, formerly head of the state-owned Bank of Ceylon, the country largest commercial bank.

Government statistics show unemployment at 12.7 percent. Analysts say the figure is of concern as it was unemployment which helped spark a southern revolt in the late 1980s when youths turned their guns on ordinary people and brought normal life to a virtual standstill.

PSID was set up in April 1996 with credit lines being available in November for BOO (build operate own) and BOT (build operate transfer) projects. The bulk of its funds -- $70 million -- is from the World Bank, which has promised to top up resources depending on disbursements.

"We also have a commitment for $14 million from Germany, and are negotiating for $50 million each from the Asian Development Bank and Japan, which should be available in early 1997," Nanayakkara said.
Multilateral agencies were no longer keen to assist infrastructure development through the public sector, due to apathy and wastage, she said.

To qualify for PSID assistance a project has to have equity of at least 20 percent. PSID will lend up to a maximum of 40 percent of the balance debt component, which can be used to finance new plant, equipment and machinery.
The projects must be a national priorities, and the borrower should have a have a letter of intent from the government.

Repayment can take up to 22 years with an eight-year grace period. The foreign currency loans come at a cost of about three percent over LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate), with the borrower carrying the foreign currency risk.
One of PSID's first clients is the Pacific & Orient Steam Navigation Co and John Keells Holdings Ltd joint venture, which is involved in a $650 million project to develop Colombo Port.
"It is useful to have an organisation like PSID. There is no other source for the long-term debt needed for infrastructure development," said Ken Balendra, chairman of John Keells.
Sri Lanka has a dearth of long-term funds and until recently even banks relied on costly short-term debt to meet long-term commitments.
One-year Treasury bills are still the longest available instrument until the Central Bank issues three-year T-bonds in early 1997.
Sri Lanka's first two private fixed telephone companies, Suntel and Lanka Bell, have also sought PSID assistance.
PSID will be officially launched locally and in Singapore in early 1997.
